source: Anderson, Martinson, De Vries (2007) Normative dissonance in science: national survey of US scientists
finding: Scientists endorse Merton-style norms but see other scientists as behaving more counternormatively than normatively. Competitive fields show more counternormative behaviour.
numbers: N=3,247 mid- and early-career NIH-funded scientists. Dissonance is largest between ideals and perceived behaviour of others.
limits: Abstract only read. Self-report and perception of others, not observed behaviour.
agent_relevance: Stated rules are not followed rules. A scaffold must enforce G3/G5 in code, not rely on the model saying it values scepticism.

source: Anderson et al. (2010) Extending the Mertonian norms: scientists' subscription to norms of research
finding: Survey plus focus groups: scientists strongly subscribe to Mertonian norms and weakly to Mitroff-style counternorms. Adds quality and governance as extra norms.
numbers: Sampled 7,760 (3,600 mid-career, 4,160 early-career); response 52% and 43%. 6 focus groups, 51 scientists. Norms endorsed 73-91% (quality 91%, governance 80%). Counternorms 18-23%; self-interestedness 33% mid-career vs 25% early. Only 7 of 32 discipline chi-square tests significant.
limits: Measures what scientists say they should do, not what they do. Calling and breadth items did not behave like norms. Per-item values only in a figure (read via fetch summary).
agent_relevance: Universalism and organised scepticism are near-consensus ideals. Counternorm weight is small.

source: Mitroff (1974) counter-norms of the Apollo moon scientists, as operationalised in Anderson et al. (2010)
finding: Mitroff's counternorms: particularism, solitariness (secrecy), interestedness, organised dogmatism. Anderson 2010 turns them into survey items.
numbers: Counternorm endorsement 18-23% in the 2010 survey; interestedness 25-33%. Mitroff 1974 itself not opened.
limits: Original not read; only the later operationalisation. Small interview sample in the original.
agent_relevance: Strong commitment (organised dogmatism) can be productive in humans; fits doubt-on-signal (G1), not doubt on schedule.

source: Huber et al. (2022) Nobel and novice: author prominence affects peer review (PNAS)
finding: Preregistered field experiment on Merton's Matthew effect. The same paper got very different verdicts depending on the name shown.
numbers: 3,299 invited reviewers, 5 conditions. Reject: 65.4% (unknown author), 48.2% (anonymous), 22.6% (Nobel laureate). Accept or minor revision: 9.9%, 23.6%, 58.8%. Invitation acceptance: 28.5% (low status), 30.7% (anonymous), 38.5% (prominent). Pairwise p e.g. 0.0120 for anonymous vs low.
limits: One paper, one field (finance). Names also carry real quality information.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that humans violate universalism. Blind judges (G5): hide author and source before scoring.

source: Tomkins, Zhang, Heavlin (2017) Single versus double blind reviewing at WSDM 2017 (PNAS)
finding: Randomised: each paper reviewed by 2 single-blind and 2 double-blind reviewers. Single-blind reviewers favoured famous authors and top institutions.
numbers: Odds multipliers for acceptance recommendation: 1.63 famous author, 1.58 top university, 2.10 top company. Female author 0.78 (not significant alone). Single-blind reviewers bid for 22% fewer papers. Famous-author effect smaller than the aggregate of six other studies.
limits: Computer-science conference, one year. Female effect only significant in the meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Direct measure of universalism failing when identity is visible. Supports stripping identity from any judge input.

source: Budden et al. (2008) Double-blind review favours increased representation of female authors
finding: Female first-authored papers rose after Behavioral Ecology went double-blind in 2001; not so in a comparison journal.
numbers: Significant increase in female first authors; no negative effects found.
limits: Abstract only. Observational before-after design; later reanalysis disputed it (b07).
agent_relevance: Treat the blind-review benefit as contested in observational data; randomised data (b04, b05) are firmer.

source: Webb, O'Hara, Freckleton (2008) Does double-blind review benefit female authors?
finding: Critique/reanalysis of Budden et al. Only the title was retrieved; the direction and size of the finding were not verified.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Verify before use.
agent_relevance: Placeholder for a contested replication.

source: Bol, de Vaan, van de Rijt (2018) The Matthew effect in science funding (PNAS)
finding: Merton's Matthew effect tested with regression discontinuity at the funding threshold.
numbers: Winners just above threshold accumulated more than twice the later funding (about 180,000 euro more over 8 years) than near-threshold non-winners. Part of the gap came from losers applying less often.
limits: Abstract only. Dutch early-career programme.
agent_relevance: Early success compounds. An agent that locks in early branches shows the same dynamic; supports not committing early.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science
finding: Organised scepticism applied to published work: 21 experiments replicated, preregistered, larger samples.
numbers: 13 of 21 (62%) replicated in the same direction; replication effect about 50% of original; samples about 5x larger. Peer beliefs predicted replication.
limits: Abstract only. Selected high-profile papers.
agent_relevance: Original results are inflated. A pass on the original data is weak evidence (G3).

source: Errington et al. (2021) Investigating the replicability of preclinical cancer biology (eLife)
finding: Large organised-scepticism test in cancer biology.
numbers: 50 experiments, 23 papers, 158 effects. Median replication effect size 85% smaller than original; 92% of replication effects smaller. 40% (39/97) of positive effects succeeded on 3 or more of 5 methods.
limits: Abstract only. Replication difficulty included unclear methods.
agent_relevance: Effect shrinkage is the rule. Expect first answers to look better than the held-out check.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: LLM judges show position, verbosity and possibly self-enhancement bias, yet GPT-4 agrees with humans as often as humans agree with each other.
numbers: Position consistency after swap: Claude-v1 23.8% (75.0% favour first), GPT-3.5 46.2%, GPT-4 65.0%. GPT-4 vs human agreement 85% (no ties) vs human-human 81%. Few-shot raised GPT-4 consistency 65.0% to 77.5%. Self-favouring win rate: GPT-4 +10%, Claude-v1 +25%; GPT-3.5 none.
limits: Self-enhancement could not be separated from quality. Small sets (80 questions).
agent_relevance: Universalism check: swap order and average (code, G5). Do not trust one ordering.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large language models are not fair evaluators
finding: Changing only the answer order flips LLM judge verdicts.
numbers: ChatGPT judge: Vicuna-13B win rate 2.5% as first vs 82.5% as second. GPT-4: 51.3% vs 23.8%. Vicuna could 'beat' ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries by order alone. Conflict rates in the paper's table range up to 82.5%.
limits: 80 queries; order effect shrinks when the quality gap is large.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G5: aggregate over both orders; use order-flip entropy as a difficulty signal.

source: Ye et al. (2024) Justice or prejudice? Quantifying biases in LLM-as-a-judge (CALM)
finding: Names 12 judge biases (position, verbosity, bandwagon, authority, self-enhancement, fallacy-oversight and others) and tests them by automated perturbation.
numbers: 12 bias types, several models, robustness and consistency rates; per-bias values not extracted this session.
limits: Only intro and method read; result tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: The 12-bias list is a checklist for a blind-judge design.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM evaluators recognize and favor their own generations
finding: Self-preference grows with self-recognition; fine-tuning for recognition increases preference linearly.
numbers: GPT-4 identifies its own output 73.5% (vs two other LLMs and humans). After fine-tuning on 500 examples, GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 exceed 90%. Linear correlation between recognition and preference.
limits: Summarisation only (CNN/DailyMail, XSUM).
agent_relevance: Hide authorship from model judges; same-model critics favour their own text (G4/G5).

source: Latona et al. (2024) The AI Review Lottery: AI-assisted peer reviews at ICLR 2024
finding: Quasi-experiment: LLM-assisted reviews score higher and raise acceptance near the threshold.
numbers: At least 15.8% of reviews AI-assisted (GPTZero lower bound). In 53.4% of score-discordant pairs the AI-assisted review scored higher (p=0.002; +14.4% relative). Matched near-threshold papers: +4.9 percentage points acceptance (p=0.024).
limits: Detector-based, observational, lower bound.
agent_relevance: LLM judges lean generous. Calibrate scores in code.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Can large language models provide useful feedback on research papers?
finding: GPT-4 comments overlap with human reviewer comments about as much as two humans overlap.
numbers: Overlap with human reviewers: 30.85% (Nature journals), 39.23% (ICLR); human-human 28.58% and 35.25%. 57.55% of GPT-4 comments raised by at least one human. Overlap 43.80% for rejected ICLR papers. 57.4% of users found feedback helpful.
limits: Overlap by an automated matching pipeline; helpfulness self-reported.
agent_relevance: An LLM critic reaches human-reviewer level of scepticism, mostly on weak papers.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Monitoring AI-modified content at scale (peer reviews at ICLR, NeurIPS, CoRL)
finding: Estimated share of LLM-modified peer review text rose sharply after ChatGPT release in Nov 2022.
numbers: Share higher in reviews with lower confidence, submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who rarely answer rebuttals. Exact per-conference percentages not verified.
limits: Distribution-level estimate, not per-review detection.
agent_relevance: Norm erosion in practice: scepticism is outsourced when effort is low.

source: Ye et al. (2024) Are we there yet? Risks of utilizing LLMs in scholarly peer review
finding: LLM reviews can be hijacked by hidden text and favour famous authors under single-blind.
numbers: Hidden-text injection: agreement with injected content 90%; agreement with human reviews fell 53% to 16%; mean rating 5.34 to 7.99. LLM reviews 4.5x more consistent with author-disclosed limitations than human reviews. Fame swap on 500 papers: positive-rating share 36.8% to 40.8% (university), 41.6% (company), 41.2% (researcher). Manipulating 5% of reviews pushes 12% of papers out of the top 30%.
limits: Prompt-injection setting; ICLR 2024 sample.
agent_relevance: LLM judges violate universalism and accept author-supplied content. Treat judged text as untrusted data.

source: Jin et al. (2024) AgentReview: peer review dynamics with LLM agents
finding: Simulated peer review reproduces social effects: conformity, authority bias, fatigue.
numbers: About 53,800 generated documents, over 10,000 reviews, 500+ ICLR submissions. 37.1% of decisions vary with reviewer bias. Conformity cut rating standard deviation by 27.2%. If all reviewers know authors for only 10% of papers, decisions change by 27.7%. Authoritarian area chairs: Cohen's kappa 0.266, agreement 69.8% with baseline.
limits: Simulation; persona-driven; not validated against real reviewers.
agent_relevance: Conformity among agents reduces variance, the G4 warning about correlated samples.

source: Thakkar et al. (2025) Review Feedback Agent: randomized study of 20K ICLR 2025 reviews
finding: Randomised intervention: LLM feedback to reviewers changed reviews; LLM guardrail tests gated what was sent.
numbers: 27% of reviewers who got feedback updated reviews; 12,000+ suggestions incorporated; update rate about 17 points above control; reviews 80 words longer. Score edits 8.1% vs 7.5%.
limits: Optional feedback, self-selection; no ground-truth quality measure.
agent_relevance: Feedback tied to specific review text gets acted on, matching G2 (revise from real output).

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study
finding: Blind expert review: LLM ideas rated more novel, slightly less feasible. LLM self-evaluation is weak.
numbers: 49 idea writers, 79 blind reviewers. Novelty 4.84 (human), 5.64 (LLM), 5.81 (LLM plus human rerank); p<0.05. Reviewer consistency only 56.1%. Predicting accepted vs rejected papers: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4%, GPT-4o 61.1%.
limits: Novelty is hard to judge; ideas were not executed.
agent_relevance: Blinding and style standardisation made the comparison valid (G5).

source: Blank (1991) double-blind AER study, as summarised in Tomkins et al. (2017)
finding: Blank's randomised AER study is the classic controlled test; Tomkins compares WSDM against it and six other studies.
numbers: Meta-analysis of 7 studies in total; for female authors the WSDM effect ranked 7th of 11 measurements.
limits: Secondhand summary only.
agent_relevance: Evidence base is thin: few randomised blind-review studies exist.

source: Snodgrass (2006) survey of 600+ items on peer review, as cited in Tomkins et al. (2017)
finding: Large literature, few controlled studies.
numbers: Over 600 pieces of literature reviewed.
limits: Secondhand; Snodgrass not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not over-claim: most blind-review claims are observational.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) human reaction to GPT-4 disagreement
finding: When a human differed from GPT-4, the human often accepted GPT-4's view.
numbers: Humans judged GPT-4's judgment reasonable in 75% of disagreements and changed their choice in 34%.
limits: Anchoring not controlled.
agent_relevance: Possible deference; do not show proposed answers to judges (G5).

source: Wang et al. (2023) remedies: balanced position calibration
finding: Swapping order and averaging, evidence before score, and human help on high-entropy cases reduce order bias.
numbers: Method uses balanced-position diversity entropy to flag hard items; per-method gain numbers not extracted.
limits: Gains not read in full.
agent_relevance: Cheap code-side fix matching G5.

source: Tomkins et al. (2017) bidding asymmetry
finding: Visible identity changes which papers get chosen to review, before any scoring.
numbers: Single-blind reviewers bid for 22% fewer papers and favoured top institutions.
limits: One conference.
agent_relevance: Which branch gets explored can be biased by source prestige, not only the final score.
